content.title: Safe Room Detective
content.summary: Find the safer spots in and around your home, together. Each card shares official guidance, and your family talks through which spots you already know.
content.objective: Find out which safer places your household already knows, and which ones to find together.

sources.label: EPA — Create a clean room during wildfire smoke

content.facilitation: An adult reads each card aloud. Talk about where that spot is in your home, and walk to it together if you can. These are practice cards. In a real emergency, follow official instructions, including if they tell you to leave.

activity.prompt: Does your household know this spot?
activity.reminderQuestion: Where would your household meet if you had to leave?
activity.recapBody: The best spot depends on your home. For tornadoes, Ready.gov names a safe room or storm shelter first, then a small, interior, windowless room or basement on the lowest level. NWS says a mobile home isn't safe. In an earthquake, people who use a wheelchair can lock their wheels and cover their head and neck. Some situations mean moving or leaving instead. In a flood, Ready.gov says to move to higher ground or a higher floor, and to evacuate if told to do so. Follow local officials.

items.label: Tornado warning: go to a basement, safe room, or interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Mobile homes aren't safe; know a sturdier shelter.
Earthquake: drop, cover your head and neck, and hold on. Get under a sturdy table, or by an inside wall away from windows. Don't run outside; avoid doorways.
Wildfire smoke: choose a room you can close off from outside air, big enough for everyone. Leave if officials tell you to.
Officials say shelter in place: go to an interior room with few windows if possible, close windows and doors, turn off fans and AC, and listen for news.
Extreme heat: stay where there's air conditioning. No AC at home? Know your nearest cooling center. Don't rely on a fan as your main way to stay cool.
